content.intro: In this lesson, you will study generative Model Architectures within Generative Artificial Intelligence. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Generative systems produce candidate content based on learned patterns and the supplied context. Fluent results can still be incomplete or incorrect.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Autoregressive, diffusion, adversarial, variational, and transformer-based approaches generate data in different ways. Architecture names are not interchangeable, and comparisons should use the same task, data assumptions, and evaluation.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Generative adversarial networks
items.text: A GAN trains a generator and discriminator in competition. Training can be unstable, and visually convincing outputs still require checks for coverage, artifacts, provenance, and intended-use risks.

items.title: Variational autoencoders
items.text: A variational autoencoder learns a latent representation with a probabilistic objective and can sample from that representation. Reconstruction quality and latent-space properties are distinct evaluation questions.

items.title: Autoregressive models
items.text: Autoregressive models is one of the concepts used to reason about generative model architectures. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Diffusion models
items.text: Diffusion models learn to generate samples through a process related to adding and reversing noise. Image quality, conditioning fidelity, inference steps, and misuse risks require separate evaluation.

items.title: Transformer-based generative models
items.text: Transformer-based generative models is one of the concepts used to reason about generative model architectures. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what generative model architectures takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Generative systems produce candidate content based on learned patterns and the supplied context. Fluent results can still be incomplete or incorrect.

content_blocks.code:
inputs = [0.5, 1.0]
weights = [2.0, -1.0]
bias = 0.25
score = sum(x * w for x, w in zip(inputs, weights)) + bias
relu = max(0.0, score)
print("score:", round(score, 2))
print("relu:", round(relu, 2))

content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Autoregressive, diffusion, adversarial, variational, and transformer-based approaches generate data in different ways. Architecture names are not interchangeable, and comparisons should use the same task, data assumptions, and evaluation. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: design two alternative prompts or conditions for generative model architectures and apply them to the same five synthetic test cases. Score both with a fixed rubric, record failures, and avoid judging only the most impressive output.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
